planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following last frost; Sikkim is a vigorous vining heirloom best grown on a trellis or sturdy fence to support its large fruit.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed, and train the vigorous vines up a trellis to keep the large fruit clean and well-shaped. This Himalayan heirloom from the Sikkim region of India is unlike most garden cucumbers in that it is prized for its mature stage, when the oval fruit develops a thick, netted, rust-brown to reddish skin and sweeter, firmer flesh well suited to cooking or pickling rather than fresh eating. Keep plants evenly watered through fruit set, since the long maturation period makes this variety more drought-sensitive than quick-maturing slicers. Harvest some fruit young and green for a milder, more traditional cucumber use, but allow others to color fully on the vine to see the variety's distinctive russet skin develop.

common_name: Zapotec Ridged Cucumber (Oaxacan Heirloom Pleated Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; give vines a trellis or ample ground space, as this is a sprawling heirloom type maintained by Zapotec growing communities in Oaxaca, Mexico.

directions: Direct sow in warm soil after frost risk has passed, spacing plants to allow the sprawling vines room to run or climb a trellis. This Oaxacan heirloom is immediately recognizable by its deep lengthwise ridges and pleated, almost sculpted surface, which set it apart visually from the smooth or lightly warted skins of most commercial cucumbers. Pick fruit at 5-7 inches for crisp, mild flesh, since the pronounced ridging can make overripe fruit tougher to peel and eat fresh. This is one of the regional Mexican cucumber landraces maintained through community seed-saving networks rather than commercial breeding programs, so expect some natural variation in fruit size and ridge depth between plants.

common_name: Miniature White Cucumber (Heirloom Small Round White Pickling Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; Miniature White is a compact, prolific old heirloom suited to small gardens or short trellising, grown mainly for its tiny ivory-white fruit.

directions: Sow directly in warm soil after frost and thin seedlings to a foot or more apart, since this older heirloom produces a mass of short vines rather than one dominant leader. Pick fruit at 1-2 inches, round to slightly oval, while the thin skin is still fully creamy white; left longer on the vine the fruit coarsens and loses the delicate texture that makes it good for whole-fruit pickles. Because the fruit stays small even at full maturity, plan on frequent picking every day or two during peak season to keep plants productive and to catch fruit before it becomes misshapen. This variety is maintained mainly through heirloom seed-saver collections rather than large-scale commercial production.

common_name: Up to Date Cucumber (Victorian English Frame and Ridge Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow once frost danger has passed and soil is warm; this late-Victorian English heirloom was bred for cool-summer frame and ridge culture and appreciates a trellis for straight, clean fruit.

directions: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost, or start under glass and transplant carefully where summers run cool, since this old English variety was originally developed for outdoor ridge culture and cold-frame growing in Britain. Train vines up a trellis or string support to produce long, smooth, dark green fruit with fewer kinks than unsupported sprawling vines typically produce. Harvest at 10-12 inches while the skin is still glossy and firm, picking regularly to prevent any one fruit from maturing fully and slowing further production. Up to Date remains one of the old English slicing cucumbers still occasionally offered by British heritage seed houses alongside better-known Victorian types.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Edmonson is a vigorous, productive Southern heirloom grown for its reliable yield of blocky pickling-type fruit.

directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after frost risk has passed, giving the vigorous vines a trellis or open ground to spread. Edmonson is a Southern heirloom pickling cucumber kept alive for generations by home gardeners who valued its heavy, dependable fruit set through hot, humid summers. Pick fruit at 3-5 inches, firm and blocky with pale green skin, checking plants daily during peak season since pickling types quickly overgrow and turn seedy if left unharvested. Its long history as a dooryard garden variety means it has had little formal breeding, so some variation in fruit shape between plants is normal and part of its heirloom character.

common_name: Kyoto Three Feet Cucumber (Japanese Heirloom Long Slicing Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; this traditional Kyoto-region Japanese heirloom is grown on a tall trellis to produce its characteristically long, slender fruit.

directions: Sow directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, then train vines up a tall trellis so the long, thin-skinned fruit hangs straight rather than curling on the ground. This traditional cucumber from the Kyoto region of Japan is grown for slender, dark green fruit that can reach well over a foot in length while staying tender and mild, in the same style as other long Asian slicing cucumbers. Harvest regularly while fruit is still slender and glossy, since letting any one cucumber oversize on the vine slows further production and coarsens the skin. Keep the shallow-rooted vines consistently watered, as uneven moisture is more likely to show up as misshapen or curled fruit in long types like this one.
